title: Gigabyte W775-V10-L01 Hands-on Bringing NVIDIA GB300 Deskside
gist: ServeTheHome's sponsored hands-on of Gigabyte's W775-V10-L01, a liquid-cooled NVIDIA DGX Station GB300 desktop with Grace CPU and Blackwell Ultra GPU, 1.6kW draw and 400Gbps ConnectX-8 networking; it reports over 26,000 tokens/second on a Qwen model. The text covers only the specs and external hardware, with the topology and performance sections cut off.

insights.claim: Gigabyte's W775-V10-L01 is a desk-side NVIDIA DGX Station GB300 system priced around a hundred thousand dollars, with a 72-core Grace CPU, Blackwell Ultra (B300) GPU, 496GB LPDDR5X plus 252GB HBM3E memory and dual 400Gbps ConnectX-8 QSFP112 ports.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Brings the full GB300 server stack to a tower workstation, a new price tier above GB10-based Spark boxes.

insights.claim: The reviewer says the DGX Station is not a slice of the Grace Blackwell ecosystem like the GB10-based DGX Spark but the complete and unrestrained Grace Blackwell experience, bringing the critical components of a GB300 server to a desktop.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Positions the product for local frontier-scale model development and inference.
insights.quote: the complete and unrestrained Grace Blackwell experience
insights.locator: The W775 throws a lot of hardware at the user

insights.claim: The author reports a Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Flash NVFP4 model running at well over 26,000 tokens per second, over 2.25B tokens per day, on the desk-side system.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Strong small-MoE throughput on one workstation; the intro quotes 2.25B and 2.2B tokens per day inconsistently, and the supporting benchmark section is not in the text.

insights.claim: The system is liquid-cooled, weighs 29kg, requires two people to lift, and its 1600W 80 PLUS Platinum PSU needs a C19 cable and effectively its own dedicated 20A circuit, at the limit of a single North American outlet.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Deskside AI is constrained by power circuits; deployment needs electrical planning.
insights.locator: Finally, here is a look at the bottom of the system

insights.claim: DGX Station OEMs have little design freedom beyond the chassis, which in Gigabyte's case is a standard PC tower with a decorative front panel and intake and exhaust on the other sides.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: NVIDIA tightly controls the platform, limiting OEM differentiation.

insights.claim: The two 400Gbps QSFP112 ports are fed by the ConnectX-8 SuperNIC, which also fronts the 10GbE Marvell AQC113C port, and any transfers faster than 10Gbps must go through the ConnectX-8 because the USB ports top out at 10Gbps.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: ConnectX-8 is central to the system topology, increasing NVIDIA networking content per workstation.
insights.locator: Chief among these are the two QSFP112 ports

insights.claim: DGX Station has no true integrated display GPU, so the BMC provides the only graphics output out of the box, and a full graphics solution requires pairing with an NVIDIA RTX PRO Blackwell video card.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Attach opportunity for RTX PRO cards.
insights.locator: At the end of the rear I/O panel

insights.claim: The review is sponsored: Gigabyte loaned the unit.
insights.speaker: Patrick Kennedy
insights.so_what: Disclosed sponsorship; weigh the positive framing accordingly.
insights.quote: Gigabyte loaned us this unit so we could make this content. We have to say this is sponsored.
